q: Biology is regarded as the study of living things, such as plants, animals and microorganisms.
e: True. Biology is regarded as the study of living things, such as plants, animals and microorganisms. Microorganisms are microscopic living things such as bacteria, protozoa, and many fungi. Biology systematically studies plants, animals, and microorganisms.

q: The whole world is now suffering under the impact of infectious disease outbreak and weather changes caused by the effect of global warming.
e: True. The whole world is now suffering under the impact of infectious disease outbreak and weather changes caused by the effect of global warming. Global warming is the rise in earth's temperature from extra greenhouse gases.

q: Morphology is the study of cell structure and function.
e: False. Morphology does not study cell structure and function. Cytology studies the cell; morphology studies form and structure.

q: Cytology is the study of cell structure and function.
e: True. Cytology is the study of cell structure and function.

q: Applied biology includes biotechnology, medicine, veterinary science, agriculture and animal husbandry.
e: True. Applied biology includes biotechnology, medicine, veterinary science, agriculture and animal husbandry. Animal husbandry is breeding and raising livestock, not growing crops. Biotechnology uses living systems in industry, medicine, and agriculture.

q: Biophysics applies the laws of physics to study the biological processes, like flight of the bird or echolocation in bats.
e: True. Biophysics applies the laws of physics to study the biological processes, like flight of the bird or echolocation in bats. Bats use echolocation; biophysics studies that with the laws of physics. Biophysics applies physics to living processes, such as bird flight or bat echolocation.

q: Biochemistry is the study of chemical substances and the chemical processes which occur in the cells and organisms.
e: True. Biochemistry is the study of chemical substances and the chemical processes which occur in the cells and organisms. Biochemistry studies chemical substances and reactions inside cells.

q: Biogeography explains how plants and animals are distributed on earth through space and time.
e: True. Biogeography explains how plants and animals are distributed on earth through space and time. Biogeography tracks distribution of species through space and time.

q: Biometry is the combination of biology and physics.
e: False. Biometry is not biology plus physics. Biophysics applies physics; biometry applies statistics.

q: Medicine and veterinary science are concerned with the restoration and maintenance of health in human and in animals.
e: True. Medicine and veterinary science are concerned with the restoration and maintenance of health in human and in animals. Veterinary science restores and maintains animal health. Applied biology includes medicine, which restores and maintains human health.

q: Animal husbandry is the farming of crops and breeding of livestock for food.
e: False. Animal husbandry is not crop farming. Agriculture grows crops; husbandry raises livestock.

q: Pure science branches study the basic facts or principles, such as the study of structure and function of living things.
e: True. Pure science branches study the basic facts or principles, such as the study of structure and function of living things.

q: Biology has strong links with physics, chemistry, geology, geography, mathematics and computer science.
e: True. Biology has strong links with physics, chemistry, geology, geography, mathematics and computer science. Biology also links to computer science, as well as physics and chemistry. Biology systematically studies plants, animals, and microorganisms.

q: Identification in biology is the process in which an organism or specimen is classified and assigned a scientific name.
e: True. Identification in biology is the process in which an organism or specimen is classified and assigned a scientific name. Biology systematically studies plants, animals, and microorganisms.

q: The study and process of classification is known as Taxonomy.
e: True. The study and process of classification is known as Taxonomy. Classification groups organisms so we can name them and see relatedness. Taxonomy is the science of naming and classifying organisms.

q: The classification or grouping of living things is arranged in a hierarchical order and is known as hierarchical classification.
e: True. The classification or grouping of living things is arranged in a hierarchical order and is known as hierarchical classification. Classification groups organisms so we can name them and see relatedness. Living things are placed in a nested hierarchy of taxa.

q: There are seven taxonomic groups or taxa in the hierarchical classification.
e: False. There are not just seven ranks once domain is included. Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species make eight.

q: At the top of the hierarchy are three domains: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya.
e: True. At the top of the hierarchy are three domains: Archaea, Bacteria and Eukarya. Archaea are prokaryotes, often living in extreme habitats, and are not bacteria.

q: Each of the three domains is subdivided into seven different levels or taxa: Kingdom, Phylum/Division, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species.
e: True. Each of the three domains is subdivided into seven different levels or taxa: Kingdom, Phylum/Division, Class, Order, Family, Genus and Species. A species is a group of organisms that can breed to produce fertile offspring. Older schemes listed seven ranks; adding domain makes eight.

q: Cladistics is a method of classification that uses techniques including comparing of DNA from different species to find out how closely they are related.
e: True. Cladistics is a method of classification that uses techniques including comparing of DNA from different species to find out how closely they are related. Classification groups organisms so we can name them and see relatedness. Cladistics groups organisms by shared derived characters and common ancestry.

q: Biologists usually use easily identifiable features like morphology and anatomy as keys to carry out the identification of organism.
e: True. Biologists usually use easily identifiable features like morphology and anatomy as keys to carry out the identification of organism. Morphology is the study of structure and form of organisms. Anatomy studies internal structure of organisms.

q: The word dichotomous is derived from Greek words meaning "divided into three parts".
e: False. Dichotomous does not mean divided into three parts. The Greek sense is split into two.

q: Dichotomous keys often begin with specific characteristics and then progress to more general ones step by step.
e: False. A dichotomous key starts with general features and then moves to specific ones, not the reverse.

q: In the dichotomous key for plant divisions, vascular system absent and no embryo formation indicates Thallophyta.
e: True. In the dichotomous key for plant divisions, vascular system absent and no embryo formation indicates Thallophyta. A dichotomous key splits identification into two contrasting choices at each step, from general to specific.

q: In the dichotomous key for plant divisions, vascular system absent and has spores and gametes formation indicates Bryophyta.
e: True. In the dichotomous key for plant divisions, vascular system absent and has spores and gametes formation indicates Bryophyta. A dichotomous key splits identification into two contrasting choices at each step, from general to specific. Bryophytes are non-vascular plants such as mosses.

q: In the dichotomous key for plant divisions, vascular system present and spore-bearing indicates Pteridophyta.
e: True. In the dichotomous key for plant divisions, vascular system present and spore-bearing indicates Pteridophyta. Pteridophytes are vascular, seedless plants such as ferns. A dichotomous key splits identification into two contrasting choices at each step, from general to specific.

q: In the dichotomous key for plant divisions, vascular system present and non-flowering plants indicates Angiospermae.
e: False. Non-flowering seed plants with vascular tissue are gymnosperms, not angiosperms. Angiosperms flower.

q: In the dichotomous key for vertebrate classes, cold-blooded animals with body not covered with scales are Amphibians.
e: True. In the dichotomous key for vertebrate classes, cold-blooded animals with body not covered with scales are Amphibians. A dichotomous key splits identification into two contrasting choices at each step, from general to specific. Scales without feathers point toward reptiles in simple keys.

q: In the dichotomous key for vertebrate classes, warm-blooded animals with feathers present on body are Mammals.
e: False. Warm-blooded animals with feathers are birds, not mammals. Mammals have hair and milk.

q: In the dichotomous key for vertebrate classes, cold-blooded animals with fins are Fish.
e: True. In the dichotomous key for vertebrate classes, cold-blooded animals with fins are Fish. A dichotomous key splits identification into two contrasting choices at each step, from general to specific. Fish typically use gills; aquatic turtles more often use lungs and accessory surfaces.

q: In the dichotomous key for vertebrate classes, cold-blooded animals with four limbs or without limbs are Reptiles.
e: True. In the dichotomous key for vertebrate classes, cold-blooded animals with four limbs or without limbs are Reptiles. A dichotomous key splits identification into two contrasting choices at each step, from general to specific. Four major environment components together are called the ecosphere.

q: Basically there are two main types of microscope, the light microscope and the electron microscope.
e: True. Basically there are two main types of microscope, the light microscope and the electron microscope. A light microscope uses light as the radiation that forms the image. Electron microscopes use electrons as the radiation source.

q: The light microscope uses electron as a source of radiation to form the image of the specimen.
e: False. A light microscope uses light, not electrons. Electrons are for electron microscopes.

q: The electron microscope uses electron as a source of radiation.
e: True. The electron microscope uses electron as a source of radiation. Electron microscopes use electrons as the radiation source. An electron microscope uses electrons, not light, and can magnify up to about 500,000 times.

q: Two different types of electron microscopes are commonly used: the transmission electron microscope (TEM) and the scanning electron microscope (SEM).
e: True. Two different types of electron microscopes are commonly used: the transmission electron microscope (TEM) and the scanning electron microscope (SEM). q: In the TEM, the electron beam is passed back and forth over the surface of the specimen.
e: False. TEM does not scan back and forth over the surface. SEM does that; TEM sends electrons through a thin slice.

q: In the SEM, only the reflected beam is observed and a three dimensional appearance is obtained.
e: True. In the SEM, only the reflected beam is observed and a three dimensional appearance is obtained. Observed size over actual size gives magnification. Dichotomous does not mean divided into three parts.

q: In the light microscope, usually substage illumination is the light source.
e: True. In the light microscope, usually substage illumination is the light source. A light microscope uses light as the radiation that forms the image. A light microscope uses light and typically magnifies up to about 1500 to 2000 times, not 500,000.

q: By adjusting the condenser, the amount of light reaching the specimen is controlled.
e: False. The condenser focuses light on the specimen. The iris diaphragm controls how much light arrives.

q: The condenser focuses the light onto the specimen on the slide.
e: True. The condenser focuses the light onto the specimen on the slide. The condenser focuses light onto the specimen; an iris diaphragm controls how much light.

q: The objective lens is responsible for both the magnification and resolution.
e: True. The objective lens is responsible for both the magnification and resolution. Magnification is how many times larger the image is than the real object. Resolution is the ability to distinguish two close points as separate.

q: The eyepiece lens magnifies and resolves the image formed by the objective lens.
e: False. The eyepiece magnifies but does not provide resolving power. Resolution comes from the objective.

q: In the electron microscope, the electron beam, the specimen and the fluorescent screen must be in the vacuum.
e: True. In the electron microscope, the electron beam, the specimen and the fluorescent screen must be in the vacuum. Electron microscopes use electrons as the radiation source. An electron microscope uses electrons, not light, and can magnify up to about 500,000 times.

q: The electron gun and anode emit high velocity electron beam.
e: True. The electron gun and anode emit high velocity electron beam. Electron microscopes use an electron beam, not a light beam.

q: The condenser electromagnetic lens focuses the electron beam onto the specimen.
e: True. The condenser electromagnetic lens focuses the electron beam onto the specimen. The condenser focuses light onto the specimen; an iris diaphragm controls how much light. Electron microscopes use an electron beam, not a light beam.

q: The projector electromagnetic lenses focus and magnify the first image.
e: False. Objective electromagnetic lenses form and magnify the first image. Projector lenses throw that image onto the screen.

q: The image of the specimen in an electron microscope is recorded in black and white on the screen or photographic plate.
e: True. The image of the specimen in an electron microscope is recorded in black and white on the screen or photographic plate. Electron microscopes use electrons as the radiation source. An electron microscope uses electrons, not light, and can magnify up to about 500,000 times.

q: The light microscope magnifies up to 500,000X.
e: False. A light microscope does not reach 500,000 times. That order of magnification is for electron microscopes.

q: The electron microscope magnifies up to 500,000X.
e: True. The electron microscope magnifies up to 500,000X. Electron microscopes use electrons as the radiation source. An electron microscope uses electrons, not light, and can magnify up to about 500,000 times.

q: In a light microscope, either dead or alive specimen can be examined.
e: True. In a light microscope, either dead or alive specimen can be examined. A light microscope uses light as the radiation that forms the image. A light microscope uses light and typically magnifies up to about 1500 to 2000 times, not 500,000.

q: In an electron microscope, only dehydrated and dead specimen can be examined.
e: True. In an electron microscope, only dehydrated and dead specimen can be examined. Electron microscopes use electrons as the radiation source. An electron microscope uses electrons, not light, and can magnify up to about 500,000 times.

q: The preparation of specimen for an electron microscope is simple and not complicated.
e: False. Electron-microscope preparation is lengthy and complicated, not simple.

q: Magnification is the ability to increase the size of the image of the object being studied so that microscopic organisms become visible.
e: True. Magnification is the ability to increase the size of the image of the object being studied so that microscopic organisms become visible. Magnification is how many times larger the image is than the real object.

q: The formula for magnification is $M = \frac{A}{I}$ where $A$ is actual size and $I$ is observed size.
e: False. Magnification is observed image size divided by actual size, not actual divided by image.

q: Resolution is the ability to distinguish between two objects that are close together.
e: True. Resolution is the ability to distinguish between two objects that are close together. Dichotomous means divided into two parts, from Greek.

q: An increase in magnification always produces a more detailed image.
e: False. More magnification does not always mean more detail. Without resolution the image is only a larger blur.

q: With resolution, the greater the resolution, the greater the detail.
e: True. With resolution, the greater the resolution, the greater the detail. Resolution is the ability to distinguish two close points as separate.

q: Biotechnology applies the use of living systems and organisms to produce useful chemicals and products or to carry out industrial work for mankind.
e: True. Biotechnology applies the use of living systems and organisms to produce useful chemicals and products or to carry out industrial work for mankind. Biotechnology uses living systems in industry, medicine, and agriculture.

q: Traditional biotechnology came into use thousands of years ago when people unknowingly discovered the usefulness of microorganisms like bacteria and yeast.
e: True. Traditional biotechnology came into use thousands of years ago when people unknowingly discovered the usefulness of microorganisms like bacteria and yeast. q: It was known that seven thousand years ago, people in Mesopotamia used bacteria to convert wine into vinegar.

q: Examples of traditional biotechnology include making wine, cheese, yoghurt, bread and beer.
e: True. Examples of traditional biotechnology include making wine, cheese, yoghurt, bread and beer. Biotechnology uses living systems in industry, medicine, and agriculture. In bread making, yeast produces carbon dioxide, which makes dough rise, plus ethanol.

q: Modern biotechnology produces a vast range of materials, ranging from medicines like antibiotic penicillin to chemicals like enzymes and fuel.
e: True. Modern biotechnology produces a vast range of materials, ranging from medicines like antibiotic penicillin to chemicals like enzymes and fuel. Biotechnology uses living systems in industry, medicine, and agriculture. Penicillin is an antibiotic originally from a fungus.

q: In modern biotechnology, scientists are able to modify or manipulate living organisms by transferring genes from one organism to another, usually a related species.
e: False. Modern gene transfer is not limited to related species. Genes can move between unrelated organisms.

q: Transgenic goats produce antibodies and blood clotting agent in their milk.
e: True. Transgenic goats produce antibodies and blood clotting agent in their milk. Blood clotting seals wounds and needs clotting proteins from the liver.

q: Transgenic plants are engineered to produce vaccine.
e: True. Transgenic plants are engineered to produce vaccine. Vaccines are an applied-biology tool for preventing infectious disease.

q: Microorganisms include protists, archaea, fungi, bacteria and viruses.
e: True. Microorganisms include protists, archaea, fungi, bacteria and viruses. Microorganisms are microscopic living things such as bacteria, protozoa, and many fungi. Archaea are prokaryotes, often living in extreme habitats, and are not bacteria.

q: Archaea and bacteria are eukaryotes.
e: False. Archaea and bacteria are prokaryotes. They do not have a true nucleus.

q: Protists and fungi are eukaryotes.
e: True. Protists and fungi are eukaryotes. Eukaryotes have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

q: Viruses are cellular and have the characteristics of living things.
e: False. Viruses are not cellular and do not show all characteristics of free-living organisms. They replicate only in a host.

q: Viruses can reproduce inside the living cell of other organisms by using the genetic materials of the host.
e: True. Viruses can reproduce inside the living cell of other organisms by using the genetic materials of the host. Viruses are acellular and only reproduce inside a host cell.

q: Protists are single-celled organisms usually found in the wet surrounding.
e: True. Protists are single-celled organisms usually found in the wet surrounding.

q: Fungi have hyphae or filamentous cells, but yeasts have single spherical cells.
e: True. Fungi have hyphae or filamentous cells, but yeasts have single spherical cells.

q: Microorganisms can be cultured easily by using fermenters where they can reproduce profusely as they can be kept in optimum conditions.
e: True. Microorganisms can be cultured easily by using fermenters where they can reproduce profusely as they can be kept in optimum conditions. Microorganisms are microscopic living things such as bacteria, protozoa, and many fungi.

q: Microorganisms are affected by outside conditions like climate, so they grow slowly.
e: False. In controlled culture, microorganisms can grow rapidly. Outside climate is not what sets fermenter speed.

q: The nutrients microorganisms need are quite cheap and sometimes they can be fed with waste products of other industrial processes.
e: True. The nutrients microorganisms need are quite cheap and sometimes they can be fed with waste products of other industrial processes. Microorganisms are microscopic living things such as bacteria, protozoa, and many fungi.

q: Raw or unrefined sugar obtained from sugarcane or cane wastes are used as nutrient for the aerobically respiring yeasts to make biofuel.

q: The fermentation process of biofuel production produces ethanol which is distilled to obtain pure ethanol.
e: True. The fermentation process of biofuel production produces ethanol which is distilled to obtain pure ethanol. Fermentation is microbial chemical change of organic material, with or without oxygen in modern use. Yeast fermentation turns sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide.

q: Pure ethanol is mixed with petrol to get gasohol which is used for driving cars.
e: True. Pure ethanol is mixed with petrol to get gasohol which is used for driving cars. Yeast fermentation turns sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide.

q: In bread making, water activates the amylase enzymes to act on the starch in the flour breaking it down to sugar.
e: True. In bread making, water activates the amylase enzymes to act on the starch in the flour breaking it down to sugar. Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed reactions without being used up. Amylase is the enzyme that hydrolyses starch.

q: In bread making, the yeasts ferment the sugar to oxygen and water.
e: False. Bread yeast ferments sugar to carbon dioxide and ethanol, not to oxygen and water.

q: The dough is left to ferment at about 27°C for a few hours.
e: True. The dough is left to ferment at about 27°C for a few hours. Some stages of division are timed in hours in typical cell-cycle descriptions.

q: A sticky protein gluten holds the carbon dioxide gas bubbles in the dough and makes it rise.
e: True. A sticky protein gluten holds the carbon dioxide gas bubbles in the dough and makes it rise. Carbon dioxide is used in photosynthesis and produced by respiration and combustion. Proteins are polymers of amino acids with many structural and catalytic jobs.

q: Baking the dough at 200°C kills the yeasts and evaporates the ethanol.
e: True. Baking the dough at 200°C kills the yeasts and evaporates the ethanol. Yeast fermentation turns sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide.

q: In making yoghurt and cheese, milk is first pasteurized at about 90°C to kill the bacteria in it.
e: True. In making yoghurt and cheese, milk is first pasteurized at about 90°C to kill the bacteria in it.

q: Milk is homogenized to break up the protein globules.
e: False. Homogenisation breaks up fat globules in milk, not protein globules.

q: At 40°C-45°C a starter culture of Streptococcus thermophilus and Lactobacillus bulgaricus is added to turn lactose into lactic acid.
e: True. At 40°C-45°C a starter culture of Streptococcus thermophilus and Lactobacillus bulgaricus is added to turn lactose into lactic acid. Lactic acid is the product of anaerobic respiration in muscle when oxygen is short.

q: Lactic acid coagulates the milk protein casein to produce thick creamy yoghurt.
e: True. Lactic acid coagulates the milk protein casein to produce thick creamy yoghurt. Lactic acid is the product of anaerobic respiration in muscle when oxygen is short. Proteins are polymers of amino acids with many structural and catalytic jobs.

q: In the making of cheese, a mixture of enzymes called rennet is added before the coagulation of milk protein casein.

q: Rennet causes further coagulation of the milk casein and solid lumps called curds are formed.

q: In making wine, the extracted grape juice is treated with sulphur dioxide to kill the natural occurring yeast.

q: In making wine, the starter culture of yeast respires anaerobically at first until the oxygen is used up.

q: When the alcohol content reaches 15%, the yeast cells die and the juice becomes wine.

q: The seeds are dried at a temperature which destroys the enzymes but does not kill the seed.

q: Wort is filtered and boiled with hops which give beer a bitter flavour.

q: Fermentation in beer making takes 5-15 days after which beer is obtained.

q: Louis Pasteur described alcoholic fermentation as "life without air".

q: Nowadays fermentation is defined as chemical changes in organic substances brought about by microorganisms only in the absence of oxygen.

q: Fermenter tanks are usually made of stainless steel or special alloy to withstand the corroding effect of acidic waste produced by microorganisms.
